title: Descriptive Statistics I: Normal Probability Curve, Central Tendency, Standard Scores
summary: Normal probability curve (NPC) and bell curve; kurtosis; Z-score; percentile; standard scores; mean, median, mode.
objectives: Define normal probability curve and its properties.
Distinguish mean, median and mode and when to use each.
revision: NPC = symmetrical bell curve. Z = (X − M) / SD. Mean for symmetrical, median for skewed, mode for nominal. 68-95-99.7 rule.
traps: Median is best for skewed distributions.
Z = (X − M) / SD — memorise the formula.

notes.t: A symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution of scores where mean, median and mode coincide. Also called the Gaussian curve or bell curve.

The normal probability curve is unimodal and symmetrical. Most scores cluster around the centre, with fewer scores at the extremes. Approximately 68% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three.
The degree of peakedness or flatness of a distribution compared with a normal curve.

r: Distribution is symmetrical, no extreme scores
Middle score when arranged in order

notes.t: A standard score indicating how many standard deviations a raw score is from the mean.
Z = (X − M) / SD, where X is the raw score, M is the mean and SD is the standard deviation. A Z-score of +1.5 means the score is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

Worked example: A student scores X = 85 on a test where M = 75 and SD = 5.
Z = (85 − 75) / 5 = 10 / 5 = +2.0.
Interpretation: The student's score is 2 standard deviations above the mean.
Z-score formula and the 68-95-99.7 rule are frequently tested. Median is preferred for skewed distributions.

mnemonics.title: Z = (X − M) / SD
mnemonics.text: Z = (X − M) / SD: X = raw score, M = mean, SD = standard deviation. Positive Z = above mean; negative Z = below mean.
